newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia cross-media laws outdated, says Howard.
newsitem.headline: Australia cross-media laws outdated, says Howard.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Thursday laws limiting cross holdings between electronic and print media were outdated.

But Howard, whose government is reviewing media ownership controls, denied striking a deal to give Australia's richest man, media mogul Kerry Packer, control of one of the country's premier newspaper companies, John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
"... a whole lot of people over the years have said that in this day and age of convergence, to have cross-media prohibition is anachronistic," Howard said on Australian Broadcasting Corp television.
"Whether the government ultimately decides to change those (laws) is a matter the cabinet has yet to decide, but I have made no secret of the fact that I regard those laws as outdated.
"There are other considerations that the government has got to take into account ... before we decide whether or not to make the change."

But Howard said there had been no deal with Packer, whose Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd operates the Nine television network and an extensive magazine stable, to change to rules to allow Packer to take over Fairfax in return for supporting Howard.
"This idea that it's the result of the deal is wrong," he said.
Australia's laws prevent a television operator owning more than 15 percent of a newspaper company in the same market and vice versa.

Fairfax, with a market value of about A$2.4 billion, publishes two major daily broadsheets -- The Sydney Morning Herald and Melbourne's The Age -- and the national daily financial paper, The Australian Financial Review.
Packer, whose company holds 15 percent of Fairfax, and analysts say abolition of the cross ownership limits would pave the way for a takeover bid.

Fairfax's new major shareholder, New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd, on Tuesday urged Canberra to change its investment laws to treat New Zealand companies the same as Australian firms in line with their free trade pact.
Brierley chairman Bob Matthew also said the company, which holds 19.9 percent of Fairfax, had not spoken to Packer about selling its stake.
"We aspire to be a long term and increasing shareholder in the Fairfax group," he told Reuters.
Canberra's media review is due to be completed within weeks.
